source.title: Asymmetric Valleys: Beyond Sharp and Flat Local Minima
source.authors: Hao-Wei He; Gao Huang; Yang Yuan

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices. Some figure text is flattened, so exact plotted values are not recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how batch size, weight averaging, and loss-landscape geometry relate to generalization using its own experiments and measures.
record.gate_note: The paper also discusses cited prior work on large batches, flatness, and generalization; those cited results are not extracted as rows. Figure-only curves are not assigned invented numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study reports results on asymmetric loss geometry and weight averaging, but none directly tests a supplied version. Its batch comparison changes both batch size and training duration: 200 epochs at batch size 128 followed by 80 additional epochs at batch size 32. It therefore cannot establish V5's fixed-epoch batch penalty. Its directional geometry measurements do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure or ranking of generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate with qualifications: under their shift and local-asymmetry assumptions, the authors prove that bias toward a valley's flatter side improves expected population loss and that SGD averaging can generate such bias. Their experiments support this account. They present BN as a possible major source of asymmetry and explicitly describe that evidence as preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies asymmetric directional loss geometry, SWA, batch-size changes, and BN parameter averaging; it does not use the claim versions' original interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship between SGD averaging and test accuracy differs between BN parameters and randomly selected non-BN parameters, and between networks with and without BN. Batch-size comparison also changes the schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: SWA has higher test accuracy despite lower training accuracy than subsequent small-learning-rate SGD: 78.94% versus 78.29%, 80.69% versus 76.56%, and 72.29% versus 71.46% on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight averaging can improve held-out accuracy relative to subsequent optimization toward lower training error within the same basin.

fits_no_version.finding: After 200 epochs at batch size 128, another 80 epochs at batch size 32 produces a nearby solution with better reported test accuracy and worse training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Continued small-batch training can improve generalization from a large-batch checkpoint; this experiment does not separate batch size from additional training.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors find asymmetric directions and report that SWA solutions lie toward flatter sides of the same valleys with lower test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Position within an asymmetric loss valley can be associated with held-out performance even when solutions occupy the same basin.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging BN parameters improves test accuracy more than averaging equally many randomly selected non-BN parameters, while averaging all weights performs better still.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of weight averaging depends on which parameters are averaged.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight averaging improves test accuracy in both studied ResNet-8 variants, with a larger improvement in the variant containing BN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch normalization can affect the size of the generalization benefit from weight averaging.

record.problems: The batch-size comparison changes the training schedule and does not isolate a fixed-epoch batch-size effect. Many results are presented as figures without exact numerical values. The authors describe their BN evidence as preliminary. The text notes that empirical SGD solutions may not be local minima.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying rows were left out. Several figure-based examples of asymmetric directions, loss shifts, and SGD/SWA interpolations are not separately tabulated because they do not measure a version's named construct; the plotted values are not stated numerically.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out generalization under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects with epochs held fixed; workload-dependent thresholds; controlled tests of longer training or adapted recipes removing a large-batch penalty.
Dropout interventions, small-data regimes, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 limits_scope verdict should be removed: an uncontrolled training-budget difference leaves the fixed-epoch claim untested rather than demonstrating a condition where it fails. Qualitative results stated in the text remain usable despite unavailable exact plotted values.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Fixed-epoch comparisons across workload-dependent batch sizes; language models; learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization adaptations.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations and comparison against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test-accuracy effects.
